content: Microcephaly, developmental delay, meningoencephalitis, radiolucent bone disease, and jaundice that begins within 24 hours after birth are clinical features associated with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). A laboratory-confirmed CRS case is defined as an infant suspected of having CRS who presents with at least one of the following conditions: cataracts, congenital glaucoma, congenital heart disease, hearing impairment, or pigmentary retinopathy, and meets laboratory criteria for CRS confirmation. Congenital rubella infection (CRI) refers to an infant who does not exhibit the clinical signs of CRS but meets laboratory criteria for CRS. Laboratory confirmation can include nucleic acid detection via RT-PCR or rubella virus isolation from appropriate clinical samples, such as throat swabs (preferred), nasal swabs, blood, urine, or cerebrospinal fluid. Efforts should be made to collect clinical specimens for serology and viral identification from infants during the initial investigation. Infants with CRI, even without clinical features of CRS, are typically positive for rubella-specific IgM at or shortly after birth. However, IgM antibodies may persist for up to one year, and approximately 50% of CRS cases are IgM-negative by six months of age, depending on test sensitivity. If IgM is not detectable in infants tested shortly after birth, those with suspected CRS should be retested at one month of age or shortly thereafter. For infants older than six months, laboratory confirmation of CRS should not rely solely on IgM testing if the result is negative. In such cases, serial IgG testing should be performed to assess for sustained antibody levels over several months. Infants with CRS or CRI should also be tested for rubella virus shedding using virus isolation techniques. Congenitally infected infants may shed and transmit rubella virus for up to one year and can be a source of rubella outbreaks. Testing for virus shedding should continue throughout the first year of life, with infection control measures maintained until shedding ceases. This cessation must be confirmed by two negative viral test results from specimens collected one month apart in infants at least three months of age. All countries should establish a CRS surveillance system capable of identifying the majority of suspected CRS cases. Routine CRS surveillance should focus on infants under one year of age, although some associated defects may not be detectable until later in childhood. The most common congenital defects related to CRS include cataracts, heart defects, and hearing impairment, which are the primary conditions under CRS surveillance. These conditions are most likely to be identified at secondary and tertiary healthcare facilities, which should serve as sentinel sites for CRS surveillance. To establish CRS surveillance, the following steps should be implemented: 1. Identify national CRS surveillance coordinators responsible for epidemiologic and laboratory components. 2. Determine healthcare facilities where CRS cases are likely to be seen and enroll them as sentinel sites. 3. Conduct initial and refresher training for participating sites. 4. Initiate CRS surveillance activities. 5. Assess and monitor surveillance quality. 6. Expand CRS surveillance to include additional sites as appropriate. 7. Analyze CRS surveillance data annually or more frequently if necessary. 8. Provide periodic feedback to all stakeholders involved in the CRS surveillance system. Rubella in pregnancy registries can be used to follow up on pregnant women exposed to rubella and their pregnancy outcomes, as well as to identify CRS cases. These registries should be maintained at the local level to ensure comprehensive follow-up and early diagnosis of infants born with CRS. Retrospective searches of medical records can also help identify CRS cases and establish a baseline for the burden of CRS in a country. However, retrospective cases often lack laboratory confirmation. Laboratory surveillance for rubella should include serologic testing and virus detection. Rubella-specific IgM testing is the standard for rapid laboratory diagnosis and is typically performed using commercial enzyme immunoassay (EIA) kits. IgM antibodies are usually detectable 4–30 days after illness onset and often persist longer. If IgM is negative in specimens collected before day 5 of rash onset, testing should be repeated on a specimen collected after day 5. Rubella IgG testing can confirm infection by detecting a significant rise in specific IgG levels between acute and convalescent serum samples. The first serum should be collected as soon as possible after illness onset, and the second sample should be collected 7–21 days later. IgG assays are also useful for classifying sporadic IgM-positive or equivocal cases in countries aiming for rubella elimination. Rubella avidity testing can distinguish recent primary infections (low avidity) from past infections or reinfections (high avidity). These tests are not routine and should be performed in reference laboratories. Molecular surveillance, including virus isolation and RT-PCR, is recommended to track rubella epidemiology and document the elimination of endemic transmission. Genotyping methods can differentiate wild-type rubella virus from vaccine strains. Communication strategies, including advocacy, social mobilization, and media engagement, are essential for promoting rubella vaccination and addressing public concerns. Social media and internet tools can be cost-effective for raising awareness, but challenges such as inequities in internet access must be addressed.
